newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia exports to grow, eye on U.S. interest rates.
newsitem.headline: Asia exports to grow, eye on U.S. interest rates.

text.p: The outlook for Asian exports is on the mend, but higher U.S. interest rates will reduce capital flows to the region, a monthly report by Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said on Thursday.
It said the export downturn had passed the low point and a gradual upturn was expected, with growth across Asia expected to reach around 10 percent in the second-half of the year.
This was slightly below the 14 percent average for the period of 1990 to 1996, but the export cycle appeared to be turning although at a slower pace than earlier forecast.
It said the three factors driving exports were world demand, the electronics cycle and the U.S. dollar.
The dollar's short term strength was deemed negative for regional exports.
"With regional currencies loosely tied to the dollar, real effective exchange rates have risen sharply over the past year.

"This will result in some competitive pressures against non-dollar bloc countries in the product markets, although statistical analysis shows demand is significantly more important than currency values in the short-term," it said.
The report also showed that despite the growing importance of intra-regional trade, some 60 percent of exports were destined for outside the region.
"Our forecast rests heavily on a resurgence in U.S. growth," it said, adding that the U.S. was Asia's biggest single market accounting for 34 percent of all exports outside the region.
Electronics goods exports, accounting for 30 percent of total regional exports, are still in the doldrums, though there was evidence of a recovery, it said.
It said higher U.S. interest rates should also see liquidity flows slow into the region.

"With U.S. interest rates expected to rise another 50 basis points and external deficits persisting, the scope for aggressive monetary stimulus outside of the closed North Asian markets is clearly limited," it said.
This would dampen the upswing but not stall the recovery.
Domestic demand was already improving in China, India, HongKong, Taiwan and the Philippines.
Four of five Southeast Asian countries had also been able to lower interest rates during the second-half of last year, a boost for export growth.
Indonesia has more scope for monetary easing and Singapore recently adopted an easier currency stance.
